what_its_for: Chlorothiazide is a 'water pill' (diuretic) that helps your kidneys remove extra salt and water from your body. It is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and fluid buildup (swelling/edema) caused by heart failure, kidney problems, or liver disease. Lowering high blood pressure helps prevent strokes, heart attacks, and kidney damage.
how_to_take: Take chlorothiazide by mouth, with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, taking it with food or milk may help. Because this medicine makes you urinate more often, try to take it in the morning so you are not getting up at night to use the bathroom. If your doctor tells you to take it twice a day, take the second dose no later than mid-afternoon. Take it at the same time(s) every day to help you remember. Swallow tablets whole with a full glass of water.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition. For adults, common doses range from 500 mg to 2,000 mg (2 g) per day, taken as one dose or split into two doses. For children, the dose is based on body weight and is determined by the doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still early in the day. If it is close to the time of your next dose, or if it is late afternoon or evening, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular scheduled time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store chlorothiazide tablets at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct light, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. If you have liquid (oral suspension) chlorothiazide, store it in the refrigerator and shake it well before each use. Do not freeze the liquid. Dispose of any unused or expired medication safely — ask your pharmacist about medication take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking this medicine, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and make you feel dizzy or faint. Avoid standing up too quickly from a sitting or lying position to prevent dizziness. Limit salt (sodium) intake as directed by your doctor. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and tanning beds, as this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to sunlight — use sunscreen and protective clothing when outdoors. Avoid taking anti-inflammatory pain relievers like ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) without asking your doctor first, as they can reduce how well this medicine works and harm your kidneys.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe dizziness, fainting, or feeling like you might pass out; muscle cramps, weakness, or numbness (signs of low potassium); dry mouth, increased thirst, or little to no urination (signs of dehydration); fast or irregular heartbeat; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or trouble breathing; yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); unusual bruising or bleeding; severe nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain; vision changes or eye pain (possible sign of glaucoma); or blood sugar that is higher than normal if you have diabetes.
when_it_works: You may notice that you urinate more frequently within the first few hours of taking your first dose. For swelling (edema), you may begin to notice improvement within a few days. For high blood pressure, it may take 2 to 4 weeks of regular use before you see the full benefit. Even if you feel well, keep taking this medicine every day as prescribed — high blood pressure often has no symptoms, and stopping suddenly can cause your blood pressure to go back up.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. This medicine can pass to the baby and may cause problems. Your doctor will weigh the risks and benefits carefully. Breastfeeding: Chlorothiazide passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: This medicine can be used in children, but the dose is carefully adjusted by weight. Older adults: Older adults are more sensitive to the effects of this medicine, especially dizziness, low blood pressure, and electrolyte imbalances. Use with extra caution and report any dizziness or falls to your doctor right away. Kidney or liver disease: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver problems, as this may affect whether this medicine is safe for you. Diabetes: This medicine may raise your blood sugar levels. Monitor your blood sugar closely and report any changes to your doctor.
